nameStory: The grey-headed coneflower gets its name from its distinctive center - a tall, dome-shaped disc that starts yellowish but turns greyish as it matures. The 'coneflower' part comes from this raised center that looks like an ice cream cone sitting on top of the bright yellow petals.
description: Grey-headed coneflower is a tall prairie wildflower that can tower over 3 feet high, making it hard to miss in late summer. It has cheerful yellow daisy-like flowers with drooping petals that surround a prominent oval or globe-shaped center. The rough, deeply-lobed leaves look almost feathery, and the whole plant has a sturdy, upright growth habit that makes it a standout in meadows and along roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow petals (up to 15) that droop downward around a tall, dome-shaped center that's greyish-green to purplish and can be an inch long - much taller than most other coneflowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rough, sandpaper-like leaves up to 16 inches long that are deeply divided into large, lance-shaped lobes - run your finger along them and feel the coarse, glandular texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and sturdy, often exceeding 3 feet, with flower heads held high above the topmost leaves on long stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: When you crush the disc center, it releases a sweet anise or licorice-like scent that's quite distinctive

habitat: In New England, grey-headed coneflower thrives in sunny meadows, prairie remnants, woodland edges, and disturbed areas like roadsides. It's adaptable to both moist and dry soils and is often found in areas that were once farmland or pasture. Look for it in open spaces where it can get full sun and won't be shaded out by taller vegetation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with distinctive rough, deeply-lobed leaves that feel coarse to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer with showy yellow flowers held high above the foliage. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the cone-shaped centers become more prominent and grey, often persisting into fall and providing seeds for birds.
seasonality.winter: The sturdy stems and seed heads often remain standing through winter, creating distinctive silhouettes in snowy meadows.

funFact: Each flower head can contain over 200 tiny individual flowers packed into that cone-shaped center - what looks like one flower is actually a bustling apartment complex of hundreds of miniature blooms!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with black-eyed Susan, but grey-headed coneflower has a much taller, more prominent cone center (black-eyed Susan's is flatter and darker), and its petals droop more dramatically downward. Remember: grey-headed = tall cone, black-eyed Susan = flat center.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'coneflower,' this species belongs to a different genus (Ratibida) than the more familiar purple coneflowers (Echinacea). Both share the cone-shaped center but are only distantly related within the vast sunflower family.
compareHints: Grey-headed coneflower differs from its close relative upright prairie coneflower mainly in size and flower color - grey-headed is much taller (over 3 feet vs under 2 feet) and has purely yellow petals, while upright prairie coneflower often has red or brown markings at the base of its petals. Grey-headed also has a more robust, sturdy appearance overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Its closest New England relative is grey-headed coneflower, but that species has much more rounded, globe-like flower heads rather than the distinctive tall, columnar cone.
